Before you use this map

This is a free reference tool that combines three public estimates of where the August 2016 flood reached: the East Baton Rouge city-parish estimate, the Livingston Parish flood depth grid, and the U.S. Geological Survey river model, along with East Baton Rouge flood-repair permits, today's FEMA flood zones and public parcel records.
  • It is not a flood zone determination, elevation certificate, survey or insurance advice.
  • These are estimates. A house can show dry here and still have flooded, or show water and have stayed dry, depending on its slab height.
  • Parcel, owner and FEMA data come live from public sources and may be incomplete or out of date.
  • Always confirm with the seller's disclosure, an elevation certificate, an official flood determination and the property's flood claim history.

August 2016 Flood: Where the Water Was

Three public estimates of where the 2016 water reached (city-parish, Livingston Parish and USGS), plus flood-repair permits, FEMA zones and live parcels. Click anywhere on the map for a spot report.

Type an address. You'll get whether the 2016 water reached it, the nearest surveyed high-water mark, and the parcel it sits on.
How to read this. Teal is the East Baton Rouge city-parish estimate of the 2016 flood area, compiled by parish GIS from 911 calls, fire department rescue points, 311 requests, street-level damage assessments, debris collection routes and aerial imagery; it covers the whole parish, including Central, Greenwell Springs and Pride. Purple is the Livingston Parish government's August 2016 flood depth grid, covering Denham Springs, Watson, Walker and the west side of the parish; the report gives its depth range. Blue is the USGS river model built from surveyed high-water marks, covering the Amite and Comite corridors inside the dashed line. A spot is reported as flooded if any one of these shows water, and the report names which ones. The dashed purple layer (off by default) is the state emergency office's broad 2016 reported-flooding area for Livingston Parish; a spot inside it that the detailed sources miss is reported as possibly flooded, never as dry. Orange dots are East Baton Rouge building permits issued for 2016 flood repairs (City of Baton Rouge and unincorporated parish only; Central's permits are not included). Areas outside all three sources are reported as having no data, not as dry.

Sources. East Baton Rouge 2016 Estimated Flood Inundation Area and Flood Related Building Permits, City of Baton Rouge and Parish of East Baton Rouge GIS. Livingston Parish August 2016 Flood Depth, Livingston Parish Government (converted to depth ranges at about 22 m resolution). Louisiana Parish Reported Flooding 2016 (Livingston), GOHSEP (live). Flood extent and high-water marks: Heal and Watson, 2017, USGS data release doi.org/10.5066/F79K48C1. All flood layers simplified for web display. FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (live). Parcels: East Baton Rouge Parish Assessor via EBRGIS, and Livingston Parish parcel records on ArcGIS Online (live). Address lookup: Esri World Geocoder. Disclaimer. This map is provided free as a general reference tool only. It is not a flood zone determination, elevation certificate, survey, appraisal, inspection, or insurance, legal or engineering advice, and it does not show or guarantee whether any specific structure flooded in 2016 or will flood in the future. The 2016 flood areas shown are estimates published by East Baton Rouge City-Parish, Livingston Parish Government and the U.S. Geological Survey, simplified here for web display. They may miss or overstate flooding at individual properties, and they do not cover every area. FEMA flood zones, parcel boundaries, ownership and values are pulled live from third-party public sources that may be incomplete, out of date or temporarily unavailable. This information has not been independently verified, and the publisher makes no warranty of any kind as to its accuracy or completeness. Do not rely on it to make a purchase, sale, lending or insurance decision. Before buying or selling, review the seller's property disclosure, obtain an elevation certificate and an official flood zone determination, ask about prior flood insurance claims, and consult a licensed insurance agent, surveyor or attorney as needed. Use of this map means you accept these terms.
